stemMd:
Five steel beams, labelled L, M, N, O and P, all have different lengths. The following is known.

- L is longer than M.
- N is shorter than M.
- O is longer than L.
- P is shorter than L but longer than M.

Which beam is the third longest?
explanationMd:
Build the order one clue at a time, from longest to shortest.

- L is longer than M, and N is shorter than M: L, M, N.
- O is longer than L: O, L, M, N.
- P fits between L and M: O, L, P, M, N.

Every beam now has a fixed place, and the third longest is **P**.

Check each clue against the final order O, L, P, M, N: L before M, N after M, O before L, and P between L and M. All hold.

distractorRationale.a: L is second longest: only O is longer than it. Choosing it miscounts the position or overlooks O.
distractorRationale.b: M is fourth longest, with O, L and P all longer. Choosing it ignores the clue that places P above M.
distractorRationale.c: N is the shortest beam, since it is shorter than M, which is shorter than the other three.
distractorRationale.d: O is the longest beam, because it is longer than L, which is longer than all the rest.

accessibilityText: A logic problem about five steel beams labelled L, M, N, O and P, all of different lengths. L is longer than M. N is shorter than M. O is longer than L. P is shorter than L but longer than M. The question asks which beam is the third longest. The five choices are L, M, N, O and P.

provenance.notes: Tests building a strict ordering from pairwise comparisons. The scenario and wording are original to this bank; no published TOLC or other test item was used or adapted.
